title: Check yourself: EMV and DE 55 in depth

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A risk rule should decline cards whose static data failed offline authentication, which EMV places in byte 1, bit 7 of the TVR. The developer writes the test as (tvr[0] & (1 << 7)) != 0. What does the rule do in production?

options.text: It declines the cards it was meant for, since Java numbers the bits of a byte the same way EMV does
options.says: EMV numbers bits 8 to 1 from the left, so bit 7 is 0x40; 1 << 7 is 0x80

options.text: It misses the cards it was meant for, since 1 << 7 is the mask of bit 8, a different flag
options.says: 1 << 7 tests bit 8, 'offline data authentication not performed', so the rule fires on another condition and lets real failures through

options.text: It declines the cards it was meant for, since jPOS reorders the TVR bits when it unpacks DE 55
options.says: TLVList returns the value bytes as sent; nothing reorders bits

options.text: It misses the cards it was meant for, since 1 << 7 overflows a Java byte and the test is never true
options.says: the byte is promoted to int and masked with 0x80, which works; the mask is simply the wrong bit

origin.section: 18.3. The TVR Says What the Terminal Saw, and Tag 9F10 What the Card Saw

questions.stem: An issuer's host receives a chip authorization from a merchant in another city. Its DE 55 is byte for byte the DE 55 of an authorization approved for the same card an hour earlier, and the HSM verifies the cryptogram. What should the host do?

options.text: Approve it, since a cryptogram the HSM verifies can only have come from the genuine card just now
options.says: the cryptogram proves the card took part once; a copy carries the same counter and number, so it verifies again

options.text: Decline it, since its transaction counter is not higher than the last one verified for that card
options.says: only the issuer's record of the last verified ATC per card catches a replayed request

options.text: Approve it, since the counter inside the cryptogram shows that this request is a new one
options.says: the counter in a copy is the old counter; the HSM cannot tell it is old, only the issuer's record can

options.text: Decline it, since the HSM accepts each cryptogram only once and must have refused this one
options.says: the HSM keeps no history: the same input verifies every time, as the run shows

origin.section: 18.4. A Valid Cryptogram Proves the Card, Not That the Request Is New

questions.stem: An issuer approves a chip purchase of 64.00. The terminal then reports that the card returned an AAC at its second GENERATE AC, and it prints a decline. What should the acquirer do?

options.text: Send a reversal for the approval, since only the acquirer's side knows the purchase failed at the counter
options.says: the issuer has approved and holds the amount; the acquirer must undo the approval with a reversal

options.text: Send the authorization again, since a fresh cryptogram gives the card a second chance to return a TC
options.says: the card has made its final decision; a new request would be a second purchase, and the first approval would still hold the amount

options.text: Do nothing, since the issuer saw the AAC from the second GENERATE AC and released the amount
options.says: the second GENERATE AC happens at the terminal after the response; the issuer never sees it unless the acquirer sends it

options.text: Do nothing, since the issuer's approval is final and the merchant can still complete the sale
options.says: the card has the last word at the counter; the purchase failed and the approval must be reversed

origin.section: 18.6. A Card That Declines After an Approval Leaves an Approval to Reverse

questions.stem: An issuer approves a contactless purchase and puts a template 71 script in the response that lowers one of the card's limits. When does the card run that script?

options.text: In this purchase, before its final cryptogram, since that template runs before the second GENERATE AC
options.says: most contactless kernels have no second GENERATE AC; the card has left the field

options.text: In this purchase, after its final cryptogram, since contactless kernels move scripts to the end
options.says: there is no step after the tap in which the card could receive the response

options.text: Not in this purchase, since the card has left the field by the time the response arrives
options.says: the cryptogram is produced in one tap, so a tag 91 or a script usually cannot reach the card in this purchase

options.text: Not in this purchase, since an issuer sends scripts after the clearing record has arrived
options.says: 18.5 shows the issuer putting scripts into the DE 55 of its authorization response; the obstacle is that the card has left the field

origin.section: 18.6. A Card That Declines After an Approval Leaves an Approval to Reverse

concepts: When the card declines after an issuer approval, for example because a hop changed tag 91, the acquirer reverses the approval; contactless usually has no second GENERATE AC.
A byte-for-byte copy of an approved chip request verifies again in the HSM and is declined only by the issuer's ATC record.
The TVR is five bytes of terminal flags with bits numbered 8 to 1 from the left; 9F10 is the card's scheme-specific message holding the CVN and CVR.
